newsitem.title: CHINA: China's Jiang reveres Deng, his reforms.
newsitem.headline: China's Jiang reveres Deng, his reforms.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin, who assumed supreme power when Deng Xiaoping died last week, delivered a glowing eulogy on Tuesday for the veteran revolutionary and his achievements in transforming China.

As Deng's memorial rites began in the capital, sirens and whistles sounded nationwide for three minutes at 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) as a mark of respect for the man who brought unprecedented prosperity to the world's most populous nation while keeping tight communist control.

"Grieve in silence," Premier Li Peng said, opening the memorial ceremony in the cavernous Great Hall of the People, and 10,000 of the Communist Party, government and military elite stood to attention, heads bowed.
Jiang sobbed as he delivered the first words of the paean that marks the official verdict on Deng, who died last Wednesday at 92 after ruling China for 18 years.
His voice breaking, wiping tears from his eyes, Jiang proclaimed: "The people of China love Comrade Deng Xiaoping ... we cherish the memory of comrade Deng Xiaoping."
On the auditorium stage lay the casket containing Deng's ashes, draped with a crimson hammer-and-sickle Communist Party flag and surrounded by flowers and a wreath from his grief-stricken family.

Standing in front of a huge portrait of Deng draped in black ribbons, Jiang vowed never to swerve from the capitalist-style reforms launched by his mentor nearly two decades ago and to keep China's doors open to the rest of the world.
"Reform is the inevitable road through which China will be able to achieve socialist modernisation," Jiang said.

On the trading floor of the Beijing Commodity Exchange, traders stood silently in front of an electronic screen showing live coverage of the rites for the man whose policies sliced through Maoist dogma to introduce capitalism to China.
Beijing streets were virtually deserted as citizens watched the ceremony on state television.

But in hosannas to the achievements of the communist veteran who created a fledgling economic superpower out of an isolated Stalinist backwater, Jiang glossed over what many see as Deng's darkest hour -- his 1989 decision to use the army to crush student protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Police cleared the square soon after dawn, throwing a security net over the vast arena that is a potent symbol of China and a focus for expressions of grief as well as demonstrations of anger.
One small group of people who unfurled a banner of mourning in the square were quickly asked to leave and police ushered away a weeping elderly couple who tried to lay a wreath.
Authorities were determined to prevent a repeat of the student demonstrations for more democracy that Deng suppressed after the death of another Communist Party luminary in 1989.
On Monday, television showed China's millions indelible images of their dead leader lying in state, his face pale and puffy. It was the first glimpse of their ruler in three years.
It was just the sort of lingering display of his remains that Deng -- contemptuous of the personality cult around his predecessor Mao Zedong -- had forbidden.
"Deng looked at peace," the Xinhua news agency said.
Political analysts questioned, however, whether the patriarch would have been at ease with the way his successors have handled the delicate transition period.

Jiang seized upon the eulogy and emotional displays for the deceased patriarch to remind his opponents as well as the 1.2 billion people over whom he now unarguably holds sway, that he is in charge, diplomats said.
"Under the party's leadership with Jiang Zemin as its core, carry out the unfulfilled wishes of Deng Xiaoping," read a banner hanging from a balcony in the Great Hall.
Jiang issued his strongest pledge yet to recover the island of Taiwan, an achievement that had eluded Deng and Mao.
"The Taiwan question will be settled eventually and the complete reunification of the motherland will certainly be achieved," Jiang promised.

The man who holds China's top three jobs -- party chief, state president and commander-in-chief of the armed forces -- gave assurances to the three-million-strong People's Liberation Army that they would not be forgotten as China races to modernise.
Analysts say the support of the military is essential for Jiang's survival as he emerges from seven years under the wing of his powerful patron.
